liturgical_day: Monday of the Twenty-second Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: The word fulfilled in their ears
theme: Jesus returns to Nazareth and announces that Isaiah's promise is fulfilled in him. The same gracious word that reveals mercy for the poor and captive also exposes envy, resistance, and the scandal of a salvation offered beyond familiar boundaries.
introduction: Luke brings Jesus back to the town where he was brought up, not as a private son of Nazareth but as the Spirit-anointed Christ. In the synagogue he receives the scroll of Isaiah and reads a promise of good news, healing, freedom, sight, and the acceptable year of the Lord. He then says that this Scripture is fulfilled in the hearing of those present. The claim is gentle in form and immense in substance: the long-awaited mercy of God now stands before them in the person of Jesus. At first the hearers marvel at the gracious words from his mouth, but wonder does not become faith. Familiarity narrows their sight. They know him as Joseph's son and expect him to prove himself by wonders performed for his own people. Jesus answers with the old stories of Elijah and Elisha, where God's mercy reached a widow of Sidon and Naaman the Syrian while many in Israel remained untouched. The Fathers gathered in the Catena Aurea see in this passage both revelation and judgment. Ambrose marvels that Christ, the speaker in the prophets, humbles himself to read. Cyril sees the Incarnate Son announcing the gifts bestowed through his coming. Chrysostom and Ambrose expose envy as the sickness that resents grace when it blesses others. Bede and Chrysostom finally insist that the failed attempt to kill Jesus cannot overrule his hour or his freedom. The word fulfilled in Nazareth remains living: it consoles the poor, liberates captives, opens blind eyes, and tests whether we will receive mercy when it comes in a form we thought we already knew.
hero_alt: Jesus reads an unlettered scroll in the synagogue at Nazareth while the gathered listeners move from wonder toward rejection, rendered in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and luminous geometry
closing: Nazareth shows how near a person can stand to grace and still resist it. The people hear beautiful words, see wisdom before them, and yet stumble over the ordinary history by which they think they already understand Jesus. Familiarity becomes a veil. They want the benefits of the Messiah on their own terms, in their own place, with their own claims first satisfied. Jesus does not flatter that demand. He recalls a widow and a foreign leper to reveal that God's mercy is free, not captive to local pride, inherited privilege, or the boundaries envy draws around blessing. This is still a searching word. We can admire Christ while quietly asking him to serve our expectations. We can rejoice in mercy when it comforts us and resent it when it reaches someone we consider undeserving. The acceptable year of the Lord begins where such captivity is broken. Bring to Christ the poverty you hide, the blindness you excuse, and the bruised places you have stopped presenting to him. Then ask for a heart large enough to rejoice when he heals others too. The Lord passes through the fury of rejection because his mission is not governed by our narrowness. He goes on his way, still preaching freedom, still seeking faith, still fulfilling the Scripture in ears willing to hear.

verses.text: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up; and according to his custom he entered the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up to read.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Jesus enters the synagogue as one who honors the ordinary worship of his people. Bede sees the sabbath assembly as a quieting of worldly cares so the word of God may be heard.
verses.commentary: Bede explains that the people gathered in synagogues on the sabbath so that, resting from earthly occupations, they could give themselves with a quiet mind to the precepts of the Law. Jesus' custom therefore reveals no distance from Israel's worship; he enters its appointed rhythm and fills it with his presence. The scene also teaches the discipline of hearing. The word is received where time is set apart, distraction is restrained, and the gathered people become attentive. Christ does not despise such ordinary obedience. He chooses it as the place where his mission will be announced.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:14–21

verses.text: And the book of Isaiah the prophet was delivered to him. As he unfolded the book, he found the place where it was written:
verses.author: Origen
verses.insight: The passage is not found by accident. Origen sees providence guiding Christ to the prophetic word that speaks of him.
verses.commentary: Origen notes that Jesus opens the book and finds the prophecy concerning himself not by chance, but by the providence of God. The scroll is handed to him by others, yet the place disclosed belongs to the divine purpose. This guards the scene from appearing merely ceremonial. The same Lord who speaks through the prophets now reads the prophetic witness in human humility. Scripture is not a detached document beside Christ; it bears witness to him, and he reveals its deepest meaning. The unfolding of the book becomes an unveiling of the Incarnate Word.
verses.source_label: Origen, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:14–21

verses.text: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor. He has sent me to heal the contrite of heart,
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Christ speaks as the Incarnate Son who has taken our flesh. Cyril sees the anointing and sending as language fitted to his humanity, through which divine mercy reaches the poor and wounded.
verses.commentary: Cyril is careful to preserve both the divinity and the true humanity of Christ. The divine nature, as divine, is not anointed as though lacking grace; yet the Son made man rightly speaks of being anointed and sent in the flesh he assumed for us. Through that mission the gifts of salvation are announced to the poor in spirit and to hearts weakened by passion. The verse therefore does not lower Christ. It reveals the humility by which the Son brings divine healing into the condition he shares with us, so that broken hearts may receive a remedy from within human life.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:14–21

verses.text: to preach deliverance to captives and sight to the blind; to set at liberty those who are bruised; to preach the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of reward.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: The deepest captivity is slavery of the mind under sin. Chrysostom sees Christ's liberty as release from the tyranny that commands evil and destroys those who obey.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom distinguishes bodily captivity from the worse imprisonment of the soul. Enemies can bind the body, but sin tyrannizes within, commanding evil and ruining those who submit to it. Christ proclaims deliverance from that prison. Cyril adds that the darkness spread over the human heart is removed by Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, so that those who wandered may find the path of the just. The acceptable year is therefore not a mere season of relief. It is the time of mercy in which the blind receive light, the bruised are lifted, and the captive mind is freed for God.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom and St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:14–21

verses.text: And when he had folded the book, he returned it to the minister and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede reads Christ's posture as full of meaning: standing belongs to work, sitting to rest and judgment. The preacher acts, then waits for the reward of divine rest.
verses.commentary: Bede sees more than a change of posture. Christ stands while reading because, in explaining the Scriptures written of him, he condescends to work in the flesh. He sits after returning the book because he points toward heavenly rest and judgment. Bede also applies the pattern to those who preach: they must rise, read, work, and teach, then await the promised rest. The fixed eyes of the synagogue disclose the proper beginning of hearing. Before the people approve or resist, they are placed under the gaze of the word and must decide what kind of attention will become faith.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:14–21

verses.text: And he began to say to them, 'This day this Scripture is fulfilled in your ears.'
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Jesus turns prophecy from expectation into presence. Cyril says he draws all eyes to himself and declares that the promised gifts are fulfilled in him.
verses.commentary: Cyril notes that the people wondered how Jesus knew the Scriptures though he had not been taught in the ordinary way. Against interpretations that applied messianic prophecies merely to former kings or holy men, Christ announces their fulfillment in the present. The word 'today' gathers the long promise into the living encounter before them. Bede adds that the Lord was doing great things and preaching greater ones, just as the Scripture had foretold. The verse is therefore both gracious and demanding. Those who hear must decide whether the fulfillment they awaited can be received in the one now speaking.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria and St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:14–21

verses.text: And all gave testimony to him, and they wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth. And they said, 'Is not this the son of Joseph?'
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Wonder can remain shallow when familiarity governs judgment. Chrysostom sees the hearers amazed at Christ's words yet still lowering him to what they think they know.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom observes that the Saviour's words carried an ineffable grace that softened the hearers, and yet foolishness soon reduced their wonder. Because they knew his reputed father, they esteemed him lightly despite the power of his teaching. Cyril presses the question further: even if Jesus were thought to be Joseph's son, why should that prevent awe before divine works and wisdom? The verse exposes a common temptation. Grace may touch the heart, but pride quickly explains it away when God comes through familiar faces, ordinary histories, or humble forms that do not flatter expectation.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom and St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:22–27

verses.text: And he said to them, 'Doubtless you will say to me this proverb: Physician, heal yourself. As great things as we have heard were done in Capharnaum, do also here in your own country.'
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Jesus uncovers the demand hidden beneath their admiration. They want signs arranged for local pride, as though grace must justify itself before those who claim him.
verses.commentary: Cyril explains that the proverb was used as a reproach against physicians thought unable to heal their own infirmity. Here Jesus anticipates the complaint that he should do in his own country what they have heard was done in Capharnaum. Augustine notes that Luke knowingly refers to deeds not yet narrated, so the evangelist is not confused but arranging the account for theological purpose. The deeper issue is not a lack of evidence alone. The hearers wish to dictate the place and terms of divine power, turning the healer into one who must first satisfy the expectations of home.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria and St Augustine, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:22–27

verses.text: And he said, 'Amen I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own country.'
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Christ's saying exposes envy rather than contempt for home. Ambrose sees him refusing to feed the jealousy that withholds honor from grace when it appears nearby.
verses.commentary: Ambrose says the Lord purposely explains why he does not work miracles in his own country, so that no one will think love of country should be despised. The problem is not the place itself but the envy that makes a country unworthy of the works of its own citizen. Cyril adds that familiar good things are often undervalued precisely because they are near and available. The prophet is rejected not because truth is absent, but because hearts presume ownership over him. The verse warns that nearness to holy things can become dangerous when gratitude gives way to entitlement.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan and St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:22–27

verses.text: In truth I say to you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut three years and six months, and there was a great famine throughout all the earth.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Jesus answers envy with Scripture. Ambrose says the ancient examples shame arrogant hearers and show that divine mercy has never been bound by their resentments.
verses.commentary: Ambrose hears in Christ's comparison a fitting rebuke to the arrogance of envious citizens. The Lord's conduct agrees with the ancient Scriptures: in Elijah's days there were many widows in Israel, yet the prophet's mission did not follow the lines that national pride might expect. Chrysostom adds that Elijah's word shut heaven and famine spread through the land, revealing the severity of Israel's need. The point is not that God lacked compassion for Israel, but that grace cannot be claimed as a possession. The famine outside mirrors the spiritual scarcity produced when envy refuses God's freedom.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan and St John Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:22–27

verses.text: And to none of them was Elijah sent, but to Sarepta of Sidon, to a widow woman.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: The widow's riches were not lands but goodwill. Chrysostom sees God's sending of Elijah to Sidon as a judgment on pride and a revelation of receptive faith.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom says Elijah was sent by God's particular appointment on the long road to Sidon, where a widow would feed him. Many wealthy people lived in that time, but none showed what this woman showed. Her riches consisted not in possessions but in goodwill toward the prophet. Ambrose and Origen also read the widow as a figure of the Church and of peoples hungry for the word of God. Jesus' example therefore wounds local pride in order to heal it. The question is not who can claim the prophet by blood or place, but who receives God's word with faithful generosity.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, St Ambrose of Milan, and Origen, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:22–27

verses.text: And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Naaman becomes a sign of the nations healed by grace. Bede sees his washing as a figure of baptism renewed by the sevenfold Spirit.
verses.commentary: Bede interprets Naaman, whose name he connects with beauty, as a figure of the Gentile people. The command to wash seven times points toward the baptism by which the sevenfold Spirit renews. After washing, Naaman's flesh appears like a child's, suggesting the new birth by grace and conformity to the Child given for us. Origen notes simply that the cleansed man was not from Israel. In Jesus' mouth the example pierces the assumption that nearness alone guarantees healing. The leper who obeys from outside may receive what the familiar and resistant refuse from within.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable and Origen, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:22–27

verses.text: And all those in the synagogue, hearing these things, were filled with anger.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: The anger rises when Jesus exposes their intentions. Cyril sees them enraged because his claim and his examples disturb the place they imagined for themselves.
verses.commentary: Cyril says Jesus convicted them of their evil intentions, and for this reason they became enraged. They had heard him announce that prophecy was fulfilled, and now his examples imply that God's mercy may pass beyond those who presume on local privilege. What began as wonder becomes wrath when grace refuses to be controlled. The verse shows that anger can be a symptom of revelation received without repentance. Christ's word does not create their envy, but brings it into the light. Once exposed, the heart must either humble itself or defend its pride with hostility.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:28–30

verses.text: And they rose up and thrust him out of the city; and they brought him to the brow of the hill on which their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Ambrose marvels that those offered blessing answer with violence. The causes that should have stirred love are turned by enmity into hatred.
verses.commentary: Ambrose says it is no wonder that those who cast the Saviour out of their city lose salvation. Christ had extended blessings among the people, yet they began to inflict injuries on him. Their conduct reveals no slight hostility: they forget the bonds of fellow citizens and turn what should have been occasions for love into bitter hatred. The attempted violence is not an isolated outburst but the outward form of envy and unbelief. The hill becomes a visible image of the heart's rejection, pushing away the very one whose words had promised healing, freedom, and light.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:28–30

verses.text: But he, passing through the midst of them, went his way.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Christ's escape reveals both humanity and divinity. Chrysostom says his presence among hostile men shows the Incarnation, while their inability to seize him shows divine majesty.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom sees in this final movement both the Lord's human nature and his divine power. That Jesus stands among those plotting against him and yet is not seized reveals the loftiness of his divinity; that he departs reveals the mystery of the dispensation, the real human life he has assumed. Ambrose adds that Christ suffers only voluntarily: when he wills, he is taken; when he wills, he escapes. His hour and place have not yet come. The failed fury of Nazareth therefore cannot govern the mission. Jesus goes on his way, free to heal even those who have rejected him.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom and St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 4:28–30
